div.head: Improved EMCF-SBAS Processing Chain Based on
div.p: Advanced Techniques for the Noise-Filtering and Selection of Small Baseline Multi-Look DInSAR Interferograms Antonio Pepe, Member, IEEE, Yang Yang, Mariarosaria Manzo, and Riccardo Lanari, Fellow, IEEE Abstract-We present in this paper a solution to drastically improve the deformation time-series retrieval capability of the small baseline differential SAR interferometry (DInSAR) processing chain based on the cascade of the extended minimum cost flow (EMCF) phase unwrapping method and of the small baseline subset (SBAS) inversion technique. This improvement relies on the inclusion of two preprocessing steps implementing an effective noise-filtering operation and an efficient interferogram selection procedure, respectively. The former step filters out the noise affecting the phase components of a redundant set of conventional multi-look small baseline interferograms. This is achieved by solving, for each pixel, a nonlinear minimization problem based on computing the wrapped phase vector that minimizes the weighted circular variance of the phase difference between the original and noise-filtered interferograms. This technique is very easy to implement because it does not require any pixel selection step to be applied to the exploited full-resolution SAR images, and it has no need of any a priori information on the statistics of the complex-valued SAR images. The latter step, implementing the interferogram selection procedure, is carried out via a computationally efficient simulated annealing algorithm and allows identifying the optimum set of previously filtered small baseline interferograms to be used as input for the original EMCF-SBAS processing chain by maximizing the (average) coherence values. The presented results, achieved by processing three data sets collected by the ENVISAT ASAR sensor over the Abruzzi region (Central Italy), Mt. Etna volcano (South Italy), and Yellowstone Caldera (WY, USA), demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed advanced EMCF-SBAS processing chain.
Index Terms-Deformation time-series, differential synthetic aperture radar interferometry (DInSAR), small baseline subset (SBAS).

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: D IFFERENTIAL synthetic aperture radar interferometry (DInSAR) has evolved over the years to become, nowadays, a well-established remote sensing methodology for Earth surface deformation detection and monitoring [1], [2]. The DInSAR technique exploits the phase difference (interferogram) between two SAR acquisitions collected at different epochs and provides a measurement of the ground displacement projection along the radar line of sight (LOS), with a centimeter-to-millimeter accuracy [3]. While originally applied to investigate single deformation episodes [4]- [8], the DInSAR methodology has progressively (and successfully) been extended to detect and investigate the temporal evolution of the retrieved surface displacements via the development of "advanced" DInSAR techniques [9]- [15]. These algorithms are based on the inversion of properly generated sequences of DInSAR interferograms and allow the computation of LOSprojected deformation time-series in areas that are not significantly affected by decorrelation noise [16], [17].

The advanced DInSAR techniques are usually grouped into two main categories: the persistent scatterer (PS) methods [9]- [12], which are mostly focused on investigating point targets, and the small baseline (SB) techniques [13]- [15] that also analyze distributed targets (DS). In particular, the PS methods operate on the pixels of the full-resolution (single-look) images that are representative of resolution cells characterized by a dominant scatterer. These targets are not significantly affected by spatial and temporal decorrelation [16], thus permitting us to analyze interferometric SAR image pairs also with a very large spatial and temporal separation (baseline) between the acquisition orbits. Accordingly, the interferometric pairs can be chosen without imposing any constraint on their baselines, and all of the interferograms can be generated with respect to one single common SAR scene, usually referred to as "master image."

Conversely, the SB techniques also allow the exploitation of DSs that may be affected by spatial and temporal decorrelation phenomena. Accordingly, a proper selection of interferometric SAR data pairs with limited spatial and temporal baselines is carried out. As a consequence, the selection of a single master image for all of the interferograms of a data set is unfeasible, and a multiple master strategy has to be assumed [13]- [15].

Among the SB techniques, a well-known approach is the one referred to as small baseline subset (SBAS) [13] that allows producing LOS-projected mean deformation velocity maps and corresponding displacement time-series. The SBAS technique has originally been developed to analyze multi-look (complex average) interferograms [13], and it has subsequently been extended to work with full-resolution interferograms [18], with the aim to also detect localized deformation signals that may affect, for instance, single buildings or man-made structures. As previously said, the SBAS approach relies on the use of multiple master interferograms generated by imposing constraints on the maximum allowed spatial and temporal baselines. Accordingly, the baseline selection implies that the SAR data pairs used to produce the interferograms may be arranged in (few) subsets that are separated by large baselines. These subsets turn out to be independent from each other (since no suitable interferogram that connects SAR images belonging to different subsets exists), thus giving rise to an underdetermined problem for the time-series inversion, which can be solved by searching for a minimum norm least squares solution via the singular value decomposition (SVD) method [13].

We further remark that the SBAS technique is fully compatible with the phase unwrapping (PhU) procedure referred to as extended minimum cost flow (EMCF) [19]. This technique represents the space-time extension of the original minimum cost flow (MCF) PhU approach [20] and is based on the joint exploitation of the spatial and temporal relationships among the computed interferograms. The EMCF approach involves the computation of two Delaunay triangulations, usually referred to as "temporal" and "spatial" triangulations, respectively. The former takes into account the SAR data acquisition distribution in the temporal/perpendicular baseline plane [19], [21]. From the original temporal Delaunay triangulation, all of the triangles containing at least one "large baseline" interferogram are discarded. This leads to a reduced-Delaunay triangulation, which identifies the time-redundant network of small baseline DIn-SAR interferograms to be subsequently exploited. The spatial triangulation, instead, involves a selection, in the azimuth/range plane, of the coherent pixels that are common to the selected small baseline interferograms. It is worth remarking that, owing to the existence of high-performance routines implementing the MCF problem solver [22], the EMCF approach is computationally efficient with respect to other recently proposed space/time PhU approaches [23]- [25] that, instead, require the solution of time-consuming linear programming problems.

The joint exploitation of the EMCF and SBAS procedures, synthetically referred hereinafter to as EMCF-SBAS processing chain, has demonstrated its effectiveness to detect and investigate the temporal evolution of surface deformation phenomena in different applications. For instance, it has widely been exploited to analyze SAR data acquired by the C-band (5.6-cm wavelength) sensors onboard the ERS-1/2 and the ENVISAT platforms [26]- [30] of the European Space Agency (ESA). Note also that, when these two radar systems (operating with slightly different carrier frequencies) are collecting data with the same electromagnetic characteristics and illumination geometries, the ERS and ENVISAT data sets may be also jointly exploited by assuming that they belong to independent subsets that can be easily "linked" with one another by applying the original SBAS strategy [31].

The EMCF-SBAS processing chain has also been used to generate displacement time-series from sequences of SAR im-ages of the C-band Canadian Space Agency RADARSAT-1 sensor [32]. More recently, it has been applied to the X-band (3.1-cm wavelength) data acquired by the new generation SAR instruments onboard the COSMO-SkyMed [33]- [35] sensor constellation of the Italian Space Agency (ASI), which combine improved spatial resolutions and shorter revisit times with respect to those permitted by the previous generation C-band radar sensors.

We present in this paper an advanced version of the EMCF-SBAS processing chain, which drastically improves the deformation time-series retrieval capability of the original EMCF-SBAS procedure. This improvement is achieved by complementing the original processing chain with two additional preprocessing steps, with the former implementing an effective interferogram noise-filtering operation and the latter an efficient interferogram selection, which allows us to identify the optimal reduced temporal triangulation to be exploited by the EMCF-SBAS processing chain.

The effectiveness of the proposed advanced EMCF-SBAS processing chain is demonstrated through an extensive set of experiments carried out on three sequences of SAR images collected by the ASAR instrument onboard the ENVISAT satellite.

div.head: II. RATIONALE OF THE ADVANCED EMCF-SBAS PROCESSING CHAIN
div.p: We summarize in this section the main processing elements characterizing the proposed advanced EMCF-SBAS processing chain. To this aim, we start by considering the original EMCF-SBAS processing chain, sketched in Fig. 1, consisting of the previously mentioned two steps implementing the EMCF and the SBAS procedures, respectively. As said, the input of the original EMCF-SBAS processing chain is represented by a sequence of small baseline multi-look interferograms identified by a reduced-Delaunay triangulation computed in the temporal/perpendicular baseline plane. These interferograms are first unwrapped through the EMCF technique and then inverted via the SBAS algorithmfoot_0 to compute the mean deformation velocity maps and, above all, surface displacement timeseries in correspondence to the temporally coherent pixels [19]. The advanced EMCF-SBAS processing chain, whose block diagram is shown in Fig. 2, complements the original EMCF-SBAS processing chain with two additional preprocessing steps referred to as interferogram noise-filtering and interferogram selection techniques, respectively.

The former, briefly presented first in [36] and extensively described in the following Section III, allows us to significantly mitigate the decorrelation noise effects in a sequence of timeredundant multi-look small baseline interferograms, identified by simply imposing constraints on the maximum allowed spatial and temporal baselines, by properly exploiting their temporal relationships. In particular, this result is achieved as follows: 1) by solving a nonlinear minimization problem involving only the phase information of the exploited interferograms and 2) without requiring the implementation of any pixel-by-pixel adaptive procedures for the DS identification, based on the distributed scattering hypothesis [38], [39] and applied to the full-resolution SAR images. Note that these are distinct and easy-to-implement features of our approach with respect to the phase linking approach [39], the SqueeSAR algorithm [40], and other recently proposed multitemporal interferogram filtering techniques [41]- [43]. Moreover, another peculiar characteristic of our method is the exploitation of a limited set of small baseline interferograms, which are selected by simply imposing constraints on the maximum allowed interferometric spatial and temporal baselines.

For what concerns the interferogram selection technique, which is extensively discussed in Section IV, it is aimed at identifying, starting from the previously filtered multi-look small baseline interferograms, the most appropriate temporal reduced triangulation to be exploited by the EMCF technique. In particular, our procedure maximizes the (average) coherence values of the small baseline multi-look interferograms belonging to the selected reduced triangulation through a simulated annealing (SA) searching strategy [44].

div.head: III. INTERFEROGRAM NOISE-FILTERING TECHNIQUE
div.p: We present in this section the analytical description of the proposed interferogram noise-filtering algorithm. Moreover, in order to show the effectiveness of the developed technique, we also present some results achieved by considering a data set of ENVISAT SAR images acquired over the Abruzzi region (Central Italy), which represents a very critical test-site since the related interferograms are typically affected by severe decorrelation noise artifacts.

Note that the dependence on (x, r) variables is hereinafter not explicitly mentioned since the proposed technique implies a pixel-bypixel temporal analysis.

The presented noise-filtering approach arises from the observation that multi-look interferograms are not fully timeconsistent because they are typically generated through the multi-look operation, followed by a noise-filtering step [46], [47], and these steps are both independently carried out on each single interferogram. Indeed, the sum of the three (generic) multi-look interferograms computed from the SAR images acquired at the epochs t A , t B , and t C , i.e., ΔΦ BA = Φ B -Φ A -π,π , ΔΦ CB = Φ C -Φ B -π,π , and ΔΦ AC = Φ A -Φ C -π,π , is different from zero [40], [48] ΔΦ BA + ΔΦ CB + ΔΦ AC -π,π = 0.

Our noise-filtering method is based on analyzing the temporal inconsistencies of the computed time-redundant network of multi-look interferograms; it first allows estimating the (unknown) vector of the wrapped phases (related to the SAR acquisitions), which is subsequently used to reconstruct a new sequence of time-consistent noise-filtered interferograms. The exploitation of conventional small baseline multi-look interferograms is the distinctive characteristic of the proposed approach with respect to previous solutions, such as the SqueeSAR method [40] and other recently proposed multitemporal filtering techniques based on constraining the analysis to distributed scatterers [41], [42], which are identified through a pixelby-pixel selection procedure performed at the full-resolution complex SAR image spatial grid. Such a selection permits us to rely on the distributed scattering hypothesisfoot_1 under which the probability density function (pdf) of the complex-valued SAR image may be regarded as being a zero-mean multivariate circular normal distribution, and an appropriate maximum likelihood (ML) estimation step of the filtered phase values associated to each SAR acquisition is implemented [40].

On the contrary, in our approach, we focus on conventional multi-look interferograms generated without any a priori pixel selection step. Accordingly, we cannot rely on the validity of the aforementioned distributed scattering hypothesis. This is not a limiting issue for our technique that, for each pixel of the multilook grid, is based on searching for the (unknown) phase vector of the wrapped phases (related to the SAR acquisitions), e.g., Φ, that minimizes the weighted circular variance [49]- [53], e.g., ν, of the random phase vector, namely, r, representative of the phase difference between the original and reconstructed small baseline interferograms (residual phases). At this stage, it is easy to recognize that this new sequence of multi-look interferograms Δ Φ is, in turn, not fully time-consistent as the original one ΔΦ was, although the interferogram temporal inconsistency has strongly been reduced. A few additional considerations on the proposed interferogram noise-filtering procedure are now in order.

First, we underline that our interferogram noise-filtering technique is not just an adaptation of the phase linking approach and of the SqueeSAR algorithm [40] to the SBAS context. Indeed, although these methods have the same starting point, consisting in the lack of triangularityfoot_3 among the phases due to the inconsistencies in the multi-look interferograms [see (1)], they are fundamentally different for what concerns both the exploited statistical frameworks and the mathematical formu-lation of the minimization procedures applied to retrieve the filtered interferograms. These issues are discussed in detail in Appendix II.

Second, we remark that the minimization of the nonlinear functional in (2a) and (2b) can be independently performed for each pixel of the multi-look grid by using one of the several nonlinear optimization software packages currently available in literature [54]- [56]. In particular, in this paper, we use the quasi-Newton limited-memory Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno method [55] (freely available at http://users.eecs. northwestern.edu/~nocedal/lbfgsb.html), which is particularly suitable to solve constrained/unconstrained large nonlinear optimization problems, by guaranteeing stable results and high computational efficiency.

Third, it is worth noting that, since only phase differences appear in (2a) and (2b), the obtained solution can be only estimated up to a constant (e.g., we impose the phase value of the first SAR image equal to zero). Furthermore, in the more general case that the imposed perpendicular and temporal baseline constraints lead to the separation of the available SAR data set in more than one independent subset of small baseline SAR data pairs, the nonlinear minimization procedure can be independently performed for each subset. Accordingly, if we assume to face with L independent small baseline subsets of SAR acquisitions, it is easy to recognize that the unknown phase terms in (2a) and (2b) can be now estimated just up to arbitrary L additive constants, since only the phase differences between SAR acquisitions that belong to the same subset appear in (2a) and (2b). However, this does not represent a drawback of the algorithm because, once the noisefiltered interferograms belonging to each independent subset are retrieved, the application of the SBAS inversion allows us to compute the (unknown) L -1 phase offsets among the different L subsets [13].

Fourth, we highlight that, within the minimization scheme, we use only small perpendicular and temporal baseline interferograms because the large baseline ones, which are characterized by small values of the spatial coherence w k [16], [17], are proved not contributing in (2a) and (2b) with relevant additional information. Indeed, we show in Appendix III the validity of this statement through a series of experimental tests carried out by applying the minimization procedure in (2a) and (2b) initially to the whole network of all of the possible M (max) = (N + 1) • N/2 interferograms and, subsequently, to limited groups of interferograms selected by progressively discarding the large baseline ones.

Finally, we stress that the proposed noise-filtering approach is intrinsically parallelizable by exploiting efficient concurrent and/or distributed processing approaches, thus allowing a significant reduction of the overall algorithm computational burden. This is due to the fact that the algorithm implements nonlinear minimization procedures that can be independently carried out for each pixel of the multi-look spatial scale.

div.head: B. Experimental Results
div.p: We investigated a data set consisting of 39 SAR images (Track 308, Frame 2754) collected by the ENVISAT sensor between December 2002 and August 2010 over the Abruzzi region. The test-site area includes the city of L'Aquila and its surroundings, which were struck on April 6, 2009, by a 6.3-Mw earthquake that caused more than three hundred fatalities, thousands evacuees, and severe industrial and residential building damage [33]; the amplitude of a sample image of the investigated area is shown in Fig. 4(a).

The SAR images are represented in the T × B ⊥ temporal/ perpendicular baseline plane 4 as depicted in Fig. 4(b), while the corresponding set of small baseline interferograms is shown in Fig. 4(c). The latter has been obtained by imposing maximum perpendicular and temporal baseline values of 400 m and 2000 days, respectively. As a result, we retrieved a network of 338 differential SAR interferograms that were computed by performing a complex multi-look operation with 4 and 20 looks in the range and azimuth directions, respectively [38], [57], resulting in a pixel size of about 100 × 100 m. Moreover, within the interferogram [3], we used precise satellite orbit information and a three-arcsecond Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) digital elevation model (DEM) of the region to remove the topographic phase contributions. Finally, the multi-look interferograms were also prefiltered by applying the approach described in [46].

To investigate the performance of the proposed approach, we first applied the nonlinear minimization procedure in (2a) and (2b) to the sequence of the generated 338 (original) multilook small baseline interferograms to retrieve the corresponding sequence of the noise-filtered ones. Then, we computed, by applying (3), the two sequences of spatial coherence maps relevant to the original and noise-filtered interferogram sequences 5 and exploited them to identify, for each interferogram, the coherent pixels by imposing a threshold on the minimum allowed spatial coherence value (we used in our experiments a coherence threshold equal to 0.7). In Fig. 5(a) and (b), we portray the difference of the coherent pixel number between the noise-filtered and original interferograms plotted with respect to their perpendicular and temporal baselines, respectively. The inspection of Fig. 5(a) and (b) reveals that the coherent pixel number greatly increases when we pass from the original to the reconstructed interferograms (see the diamonds above the red line), except for a very limited group (about 10%) of reconstructed interferograms that exhibit a decreased number of coherent pixels (see the diamonds below the red line). Indeed, this happens in correspondence to interferograms with very small baselines that were (originally) extremely coherent and that play the key role to "inject" coherence in the noisy ones. To recover the high-quality coherence values of these interferograms, we simply apply to the computed noise-filtered interferograms the average operation stated in (4). As a result, we retrieved a new set of (average) noise-filtered interferograms that are characterized by generally improved coherence values. This is clearly visible in Fig. 5(c) and(d), where we portray the difference of the coherent pixel number between the average noise-filtered and original interferograms plotted with respect to their perpendicular and temporal baselines, respectively. In this case, negative values for all of the computed differences are not found, thus implying that improved coherence levels characterize all of the retrieved interferograms.

To stress the interferogram quality improvement obtained by applying the proposed noise-filtering procedure, we show in Fig. 6 the original (left side) and corresponding average noise-filtered (right side) multi-look interferograms relevant to three SAR data pairs. By comparing the homologous interferograms of Fig. 6, we note that the decorrelation effects, clearly visible in Fig. 6(a)-(c), are drastically mitigated following the noise-filtering operation [see Fig. 6(d)-(f)]; this makes fully evident the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm. We also remark that the set of SB multi-look interferograms can be also prefiltered by using the filtering techniques proposed in [46] and [47]. The use of such prefiltering operations allows us to profitably increase the performance of the proposed noise-filtering approach. In particular, we show in Fig. 7 the effect of the proposed noise-filtering technique [Fig. 6(c) and (d)] when applied to the "original" interferogram [Fig. 7(a)] and to the corresponding prefiltered interferogram [Fig. 7(b)] retrieved by using the method proposed in [46]. The improvement that we obtain when we use as input of our noise-filtering technique a set of prefiltered interferograms rather than the corresponding set of "original" ones is evident.
With regard to the computational performance, we underline that the interferogram noise-filtering step was implemented through an algorithm running in parallel on several nodes.
In particular, the Abruzzi data set processing required about 360 min by exploiting five 64-b processing nodes equipped with a dual quad-core AMD Opteron 2356 processor.

div.head: IV. INTERFEROGRAM SELECTION TECHNIQUE
div.p: We describe in this section the interferogram selection algorithm that we developed to identify the optimal network of small baseline interferograms, belonging to the set of previously noise-filtered small baseline interferograms, 6 to be exploited by the EMCF-SBAS processing chain. In particular, the identified sequence of interferograms represents the input of the EMCF step, which is typically based on the generation of spatial and temporal Delaunay triangulations. Moreover, equivalently to Section III, we also present the results achieved by applying the proposed interferogram selection algorithm to the ENVISAT SAR data set relevant to the Abruzzi region.

div.head: A. Algorithm
div.p: Let us assume the availability of a set of N +1 SAR images represented through a set of points, namely, V ≡ [V 0 , V 1 , . . . , V N ], in the T × B ⊥ plane. The generic arc connecting two points in this plane and belonging to the temporal Delaunay triangulation, namely, tr D (V), allows us to identify the corresponding SAR data pair to be used for the interferogram generation. We observe that such a triangulation may involve arcs relevant to SAR data pairs characterized by large baseline values, thus potentially leading to operate with interferograms with significant decorrelation phenomena. Accordingly, to avoid these undesired effects without losing our trian-gulation representation, a straightforward solution is based on removing from tr D (V) all of the triangles involving arcs with too-large baselines, thus obtaining a corresponding reduced-Delaunay triangulation, namely, tr rD (V) ⊆ tr D (V). The identified reduced-Delaunay triangulation consists of M rD small baseline interferograms (with M rD < M), e.g., to the set of noise-filtered small baseline interferograms (Δ Φ ≡ [Δ Φ 1 , Δ Φ 2 , . . . , Δ Φ M ]) retrieved by applying the procedure reported in Section III-A.

Indeed, the identified interferograms, which may potentially belong to disconnected reduced triangulations, can be separately unwrapped by applying the EMCF procedure [19]. Moreover, the corresponding sets of unwrapped interferograms result independent of each other, but they can be easily "linked" through the SBAS inversion strategy [13]. Nonetheless, we remark that, for a relatively large amount of data, as for the case of the ENVISAT ones, the probability to obtain one single connected data set is very high.

div.head: B. Experimental Results
div.p: To illustrate the performance of the proposed interferogram selection procedure, we exploited the same ENVISAT SAR data set relevant to the Abruzzi region used for the experimental results described in Section III-B. Starting from the available set of 39 SAR images, we first generated the corresponding (full) Delaunay triangulation in the T ×B ⊥ plane [see Fig. 9(a)], from which we discarded all of the triangles involving at least one "large baseline" interferogram (by imposing the typical maximum perpendicular and temporal baseline values of 400 m and 2000 days, respectively), thus achieving the reduced triangulation shown in Fig. 9(b). Then, we applied the SA-based searching procedure described in the previous Section IV-A, by setting T (t)| t=0 = 100 and NI = 30. Fig. 10 shows the variation of the η values with respect to the number of iterations performed during the SA-based procedure, leading to the final solution, which corresponds to the optimal reduced triangulation depicted in Fig. 9(c).

To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, we computed the equivalent spatial coherence maps, obtained following the lines of ( 6), by considering the sequences of the multi-look small baseline original and noise-filtered interferograms relevant to the reduced-Delaunay triangulation of Fig. 9(b) and the sequence of the multi-look noise-filtered interferograms corresponding to the reduced "optimal" triangulation depicted in Fig. 9(c). The histograms of the three equivalent coherence maps, which are shown in Fig. 11, reveal a general increase of the coherence values. In particular, we observe that the number of coherent pixels obtained by considering the reduced-Delaunay triangulation increases by about 50% as we move from the original (blue line) to the noise-filtered (red line) interferograms. The improvement is even more pronounced as we estimate the equivalent coherence of the noise-filtered interferograms over the optimal reduced triangulation (black line); in this case, we obtain an increase of about 60%. As a further remark, we also underline that the interferogram selection step only requires a minimal increase of the computational load. In fact, on a single 64-b processing node equipped with a dual quad-core AMD Opteron 2356 processor, the procedure required about 40 min to select the ENVISAT interferograms of the Abruzzi test-site.

div.head: V. PERFORMANCE ANALYSIS OF THE ADVANCED EMCF-SBAS DINSAR PROCESSING CHAIN
div.p: We extensively investigate in this section the impact of the two new preprocessing steps, discussed in Sections III and IV, on the overall performance of the EMCF-SBAS processing chain. To this aim, we compare the DInSAR results achieved by applying the original (see Fig. 1) and advanced (see Fig. 2) EMCF-SBAS procedures. In particular, our analysis starts by considering the ENVISAT SAR data set acquired over the Abruzzi region, already exploited for the experiments shown in Sections III and IV. Subsequently, it is extended by taking into account two additional ENVISAT data sets relevant to Mt. Etna volcano (Southern Italy) and Yellowstone Caldera (WY, USA).

div.head: A. Advanced EMCF-SBAS Analysis: The Abruzzi Region Case Study
div.p: Let us start our analysis by focusing on the Abruzzi region SAR data set [see Fig. 4(a)]. In particular, we first applied the original EMCF-SBAS processing chain to the set of original multi-look small baseline interferograms belonging to the reduced-Delaunay triangulation [see Fig. 7(b)]; then, we applied the advanced EMCF-SBAS processing chain to the set of noise-filtered multi-look small baseline interferograms relevant to the optimal reduced triangulation depicted in Fig. 7(c). As a first result, we show in Fig. 12(a) and (b) the EMCF-SBAS temporal coherence maps [19] achieved by applying the original and advanced processing chains, respectively. The coherence improvement is evident as we move from the original to the advanced EMCF-SBAS maps; this is even more evident by comparing the two temporal coherence histograms plotted in Fig. 12(c). Indeed, we observe an increase of about 350% of the pixel number with a temporal coherence value greater than 0.7 (which is a typical value used in EMCF-SBAS applications [19]). Fig. 13(a) and (b) reports the mean deformation velocity maps (color) of the Abruzzi area as computed by using the original and advanced EMCF-SBAS processing chains, respectively. The retrieved velocity maps have been superimposed on an amplitude multi-look SAR image (gray scale) of the study area, wherein the zones exhibiting low values of the temporal coherence factors have properly been masked out. Note that this kind of representation is particularly effective because it provides direct information on the estimated mean deformation rate; note also that all of the measurements are evaluated with respect to an assumed stable pixel whose location is identified with a black square in Fig. 13(a) and(b). The comparison of the two velocity maps clearly demonstrates the impact that the advanced EMCF-SBAS processing chain has on the retrieved deformation products. Indeed, although both maps reveal a spatially extended deformation pattern associated to the earthquake that struck the L'Aquila city and its surroundings in 2009, the one reported in Fig. 12(b) is significantly spatially denser, thus allowing a more detailed analysis of the observed phenomena. Moreover, we report in Fig. 13(c) and (d) the displacement time-series relevant to the pixel labeled as P1 in Fig. 13(a) and (b), which is located in the area of maxi-mum coseismic LOS-projected deformation; both plots clearly show the deformation signal associated to the occurred seismic event [33]. In Fig. 13(e) and (f), we report the deformation time-series for the two pixels labeled as P2 in Fig. 13(a) and (b), located in an area that can be investigated by the advanced EMCF-SBAS processing chain only. From the plot inspection, it is clear that no significant differences are found in the deformation time-series for those pixels located in the areas where the coherent pixel density is high, also without applying the advanced processing chain [as for the pixel P1 in Fig. 13 Fig. 13(a) and(b)]. This finding clearly emphasizes the impact on the final result of the proposed advanced EMCF-SBAS processing chain, and above all, it shows that the presented advanced processing chain is extremely robust, also in the presence of strongly nonlinear deformation, as for the Abruzzi case study.

div.head: B. Advanced EMCF-SBAS Analysis: The Mt. Etna Volcano Case Study
div.p: The second case study is represented by Mt. Etna, one of the most active volcanoes in the world, for which an archive of 34 ENVISAT SAR images (Track 222, Frame 2853) collected between August 2003 and August 2010 was exploited; the amplitude of a sample image of the investigated area is shown in Fig. 14(a). The SAR data distribution in the T × B ⊥ plane is depicted in Fig. 14(b), while the corresponding set of small baseline interferograms, obtained by imposing maximum perpendicular and temporal baseline values of 400 m and 2000 days, respectively, is shown in Fig. 14(c). As a result, we retrieved a network of 288 small baseline interferograms that were computed, as for the Abruzzi region case study, by performing complex multi-look (with 4 and 20 looks in the range and azimuth directions, respectively [38], [57]) and prefiltering (by using the approach described in [46]) operations.

We applied the advanced EMCF-SBAS processing chain to this sequence of interferograms. Accordingly, we first retrieved through the noise-filtering procedure (described in Section III) the corresponding sequence of noise-filtered interferograms. Just to illustrate the effectiveness of the noise-filtering algorithm, we show in Fig. 15 a selection of original (left side) and noise-filtered (right side) interferograms; the comparison of the homologous interferograms reveals a very significant coherence improvement, which is particularly evident in correspondence to the summit and seaside slopes of the volcano. Subsequently, we applied the interferogram selection procedure (reported in Section IV) to the computed noise-filtered interferograms; this allowed us to identify the optimal reduced triangulation of small baseline multi-look interferograms depicted in Fig. 14(d), representing the input of the EMCF-SBAS processing chain.

As a final result, we retrieved the displacement time-series and the mean deformation velocity map of the study area in correspondence to the pixels characterized by temporal coherence values greater than 0.7. To investigate the deformation product quality improvement gained owing to the application of the advanced EMCF-SBAS processing chain, we compared the computed mean deformation velocity map depicted in Fig. 16(b) to the one obtained by applying the original EMCF-SBAS processing chain and shown in Fig. 16(a). As for the Abruzzi region case study, the exploitation of the advanced EMCF-SBAS procedure has led to a considerable increase of the total number of coherent pixels, corresponding, in this case, to about 40%. The two velocity maps show a very complex deforming scenario characterizing Mt. Etna volcano. To provide evidences of the temporal evolution of the ongoing deformation phenomena, we present the retrieved displacement time-series computed in correspondence to the pixels labeled as P1, P2, P3, and P4 and identified via black stars in Fig. 16(b) in the plots of Fig. 16(c)-(f), respectively.

div.head: C. Advanced EMCF-SBAS Analysis: The Yellowstone Caldera Case Study
div.p: As a final experiment, we focus on the Yellowstone Caldera, representing one of the largest and most active volcanic systems in the world. We analyzed the temporal evolution of the surface deformation occurring in the area by applying the implemented advanced EMCF-SBAS processing chain to a 17(a), whereas the corresponding set of 122 small baseline interferograms 9is shown in Fig. 17(b); note that they have been selected, as for the two previous case studies, by imposing maximum perpendicular and temporal baseline values of 400 m and 2000 days, respectively.

As a first result, we present in Fig. 18 two noise-filtered interferograms (right side) that have been compared to the corresponding original ones (left side); the comparison of the homologous interferograms makes it evident the effectiveness of the noise-filtering procedure, which allows us to significantly improve the spatial coherence of the computed interferograms. Indeed, in Fig. 18(c) and(d), the fringes associated to the caldera activity are easily recognizable at variance with what are shown in Fig. 18(a) and (b). For the sake of brevity, in the following, we only present the results that we achieved by exploiting the advanced EMCF-SBAS processing chain without comparing them to the ones obtained by using the original EMCF-SBAS processing chain. Accordingly, we portray in Fig. 19(a) the retrieved advanced EMCF-SBAS mean deformation velocity map, which allows us to retrieve the very complex deformation scenario affecting the caldera region and its surroundings, where uplift effects and broad subsidence patterns characterize the detected deformation field. In addition, in Fig. 19(b)-(e), we report the deformation time-series relevant to four pixels whose locations are identified by the black stars labeled as P1, P2, P3, and P4 in Fig. 19(a).

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: We have presented in this paper an advanced version of the EMCF-SBAS processing chain for the generation of ground deformation maps and corresponding time-series. The key elements of our approach are two additional preprocessing steps implementing an effective interferogram noise-filtering technique and an optimal interferogram selection operation, respectively.

The former step permits us to drastically mitigate the decorrelation noise artifacts affecting a sequence of time-redundant multi-look small baseline interferograms by properly exploiting their temporal relationships. This is straightforwardly carried out by solving a nonlinear minimization problem that exploits the phase information of conventional multi-look small baseline interferograms only, without requiring the implementation of any pixel selection procedure at the full spatial resolution scale and with no need of a priori information on the statistics of the involved complex-valued SAR images.

The latter step is aimed at identifying an optimal network of small baseline interferograms forming a reduced triangulation in the temporal/perpendicular baseline plane, to be efficiently used by the exploited EMCF technique. In particular, the interferogram selection is carried out via the maximization of the (average) equivalent coherence values of the small baseline multi-look interferograms belonging to the reduced triangulation and exploits a SA searching strategy.

The effectiveness of the implemented advanced EMCF-SBAS processing chain has fully been demonstrated by extensively investigating three sets of real SAR data acquired by the ENVISAT sensor over three regions where complex surface deformation scenarios are present.

It is worth remarking that the proposed advanced EMCF-SBAS processing chain can be profitably used to analyze SAR data acquired over regions that represent critical test-sites since the interferograms computed over them are affected by severe decorrelation noise artifacts. The proposed approach can be particularly relevant for the valorization of the large archives of SAR images acquired by the first generation C-band (ERS-1/2, ENVISAT, and RADARSAT-1) SAR sensors. Moreover, the impact of the presented procedure on the SAR data acquired by the new X-band (COSMO-SkyMed and TerraSAR-X) systems is worth for future analyses.

As a final remark, we stress that the proposed advanced EMCF-SBAS processing chain is rather straightforward to implement since it only requires complementing the original EMCF-SBAS chain with two additional preprocessing steps. Nevertheless, to allow an easy upgrade of the existing processing chains, based on the exploitation of small baseline multi-look interferograms, we developed two user-friendly Interactive Data Language routines implementing the proposed interferogram noise-filtering and selection routines; the relevant source codes are freely available at (http://www.irea.cnr.it/en/ index.php?option=com_k2&view=item&layout=item&id= 505&Itemid=171).

div.head: APPENDIX II
div.p: We discuss in this appendix the similarities and key differences among the noise-filtering technique presented in Section III and those proposed in the phase triangulation [39] and SqueeSAR [40] algorithms.

The main similarity of these methods is relevant to their starting point. Indeed, this is the same as that for [40] and consists in the lack of triangularity among the interferometric phases due to the inconsistencies in the multi-look interferograms, which is expressed through (1). However, we also remark that the aforementioned lack of triangularity information was already addressed and exploited within the InSAR context, well before the publication of [40]. In particular, the lack of triangularity among the multi-look phases was first investigated and exploited in [19, eqs. ( 9) and ( 10)] within the temporal PhU strategy adopted to unwrap a sequence of M multi-look interferograms.

Note also that the aforementioned phase inconsistency information was also fully investigated in the 2007 Pepe's Ph.D. Thesis (freely downloadable at the following Internet address http://www.fedoa.unina.it/1572/1/Pepe_Ingegneria_ Elettronica_e_delle_Telecomunicazioni.pdf) that has subsequently been published in 2009 [47].

Despite the previously discussed similarity, we remark that there are fundamental differences among our approach and those presented in [39] and [40], for what concerns the exploited statistical frameworks and the mathematical formulation of the minimization procedures applied to retrieve the filtered interferograms.

To fully clarify these issues, let us start our discussion by considering [39, Sec. II]; it describes a SAR data model based on the hypothesis of distributed scattering, under which "the pdf of the data may be regarded as being a zero-mean multivariate circular normal distribution." Under the validity of this hypothesis, a pixel-by-pixel (at the full resolution scale) statistical analysis is then needed to identify on the SAR images the distributed scatterers (DS) with a statistically homogeneous behavior. In particular, a small neighborhood (denoted by Ω) of pixels centered at the same slant rangeazimuth location in each single-look SAR image is considered. Under the assumption that all of the pixels falling inside Ω are statistically homogeneous (i.e., "all of the unknown phases as well the coherences are constant inside Ω"), their complete statistical characterization only requires the calculation of the covariance matrix [39, eq. ( 5)]. Using such a statistical model, an ML procedure is subsequently implemented. This leads to the calculation of the pdf of the data conditioned on the interferometric phases [39, eq. ( 6)] and, finally, to the ML estimate of the interferometric phases achieved in [39, eq. (12)]. This equation is essentially the same reported in [40, eq. ( 13)].

Therefore, both the phase Linking [39] and the phase triangulation of the SqueeSAR [40] algorithms require a preliminary identification of the statistically homogeneous pixels (SHPs) on the full-resolution range-azimuth grid. In particular, in [40], the selection strategy of these pixels is based on the application of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test to carefully select a homogeneous statistical population. Clearly, this requires working at the full resolution spatial scale and implies the analysis of the amplitude values of the complex SAR image pixels.

Let us now consider the statistical framework of our noisefiltering technique. In this case, as said, we exploit conventional multi-look interferograms that are generated by averaging all of the pixels, e.g., N , falling inside a region Ω. Accordingly, at variance with what is assumed in [39] and implemented in [40], we do not carry out any a priori selection of the homogeneous pixels that share the same statistical characteristics. As a consequence, the computed multi-look interferograms are characterized by statistics that significantly deviate (see [59] and [60] for an extensive discussion) from those exploited by [39] and [40], which are only valid if the SHPs are preliminarily identified.
Accordingly, our approach and the ones discussed in [39] and [40] are fundamentally different for what concerns the exploited statistical frameworks.
Let us now concentrate on the mathematical formulation of the minimization procedures applied to retrieve the filtered interferograms.

To do this, we highlight that the proposed noise-filtering approach is based on searching for the acquisition phases, namely, Φ, which allow minimizing the weighted circular variance, namely, ν, of the residual interferograms, which is the difference between the (multi-look) original ΔΦ and reconstructed Δ Φ interferograms [see (2a) and (2b) that are reported here for the sake of completeness
